extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers in media studies, political communication, history, and journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, classifying, and understanding propaganda: its definitions, typical design features, common techniques, media and historical uses, and ethical/intentional considerations for evaluating persuasive communication. Useful for analyzing political messaging, wartime information, advertising, and computational disinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda (general definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication that is primarily used to influence or persuade an audience to further an agenda, which may not be objective and may selectively present facts or use loaded language to produce an emotional rather than a rational response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a baseline test for whether a communication is propaganda: check for purposeful influence, selective facts, and emotionally-loaded wording rather than neutral presentation. Examples include posters, pamphlets, films, radio/TV broadcasts, websites and social media content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harold Lasswell definition
rubrics_metrics.description: "The expression of opinions or actions carried out deliberately by individuals or groups with a view to influencing the opinions or actions of other individuals or groups for predetermined ends and through psychological manipulations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes deliberate intent and psychological manipulation as hallmarks; use when evaluating messaging aimed at engineered changes in opinion or behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renee Hobbs's four characteristic design features
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary propaganda often: (1) activates strong emotions; (2) simplifies information; (3) appeals to the hopes, fears, and dreams of a targeted audience; and (4) attacks opponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four features are practical indicators for spotting modern propaganda, especially online and social-media content. Check messaging for emotional framing, information reduction/oversimplification, targeted appeals, and explicit attacks on rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Richard Alan Nelson / systematic purposeful persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda is a systematic form of purposeful persuasion that attempts to influence the emotions, attitudes, opinions, and actions of specified target audiences for ideological, political or commercial purposes through the controlled transmission of one-sided messages (which may or may not be factual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights process and target-orientation: look for one-sided control of transmission (which channels, who controls distribution) and whether messages are tailored to specific audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: White / grey / black propaganda classification
rubrics_metrics.description: White propaganda openly discloses its source and intent; grey propaganda has ambiguous or non-disclosed source/intent; black propaganda purports to be published by the enemy or another organization besides its actual origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to evaluate transparency and likely ethical/legal implications. Consider how disclosure (or impersonation) affects credibility and potential backlash when revealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firehose of Falsehood (modern characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: A modern pattern where a large number of messages are broadcast rapidly, repetitively, and continuously over multiple channels without regard for truth or consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for high-volume, multi-channel, repetitive messaging that sacrifices consistency/truth for saturation. Often enabled by social media, bots, and coordinated accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda techniques (rhetorical devices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common techniques include name calling, bandwagon, glittering generalities, cherry picking, false balance, false dilemma, loaded language, demonizing the enemy, weasel words, slogans, spin, scapegoating, and many others identified historically and in technique lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a text or media, map specific rhetorical moves to known techniques (e.g., 'name calling' = derogatory labels; 'bandwagon' = social appeal). The Institute for Propaganda Analysis (1930s) and later taxonomies provide inventories useful for checklisting techniques used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing propaganda from persuasion/advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: What sets propaganda apart is the willingness of the propagandist to change people's understanding through deception and confusion rather than persuasion and understanding; leaders may knowingly use one-sided or untrue information, whereas ordinary advocates may not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether deception, deliberate suppression of opposing views, or manufactured confusion are present. If so, that indicates propaganda rather than open advocacy or debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation based on intent and goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda is often evaluated by the intention and goals of its creator — ethics depend on intent and context, and propaganda can be interpreted as beneficial or harmful depending on sender, target, message, and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate sponsor identity, stated/un-stated goals, target audience, and context (wartime, election, public-health campaign) before passing normative judgment. The contested nature of the term means intent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wartime propaganda objectives and signs
rubrics_metrics.description: In wartime, propaganda commonly aims to dehumanize and create hatred toward an enemy, incite fear, justify actions, demoralize opponents, and convince a home population that the enemy has committed injustices and that their own cause is just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs include racialized epithets, atrocity claims (true or fabricated), emotional mobilization to enlist or support war effort, and systematic demonization of opponents. Cross-check factual claims and look for incitement or calls to violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational propaganda indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of bots, algorithms, fake or biased news, automated messages, and chatbots to manipulate public opinion and mimic real people in social networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect patterns such as high-volume automated posting, synchronized account behaviour, limited original content, and rapid spread across many channels. Consider network-analysis and account provenance to identify inauthentic amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media and medium as part of propaganda assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: A wide range of materials and media (paintings, cartoons, posters, pamphlets, films, radio, TV, websites, social media) are used to convey propaganda; choice of medium affects reach, audience, and persuasive technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate form and medium: visual imagery, repetition on broadcast channels, or microtargeted social-media ads each enable different persuasive mechanisms. Historical examples (posters, film) illustrate medium-specific strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising / public relations overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda shares techniques with advertising and public relations; covert forms (paid articles disguised as news) present issues subjectively to persuade rather than inform and can be considered covert propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess disclosures and format: look for paid content masquerading as news, branded messaging, or PR-style uniformity. Legal/regulatory rules (where applicable) may require disclosure when advertising is presented as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification difficulty and avoidance of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying propaganda is difficult because it must be differentiated from other types of persuasion and because evaluators risk adopting a biased approach; understanding rhetorical strategies is a necessary prerequisite to studying transmission methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt systematic frameworks (technique inventories, source verification, cross-referencing facts) and be aware of one's own biases when labeling content as propaganda. Use multiple indicators rather than a single trigger.

rubrics_metrics.name: NATO / military doctrinal definition
rubrics_metrics.description: NATO's guidance defines propaganda as 'information, ideas, doctrines, or special appeals disseminated to influence the opinion, emotions, attitudes, or behaviour of any specified group in order to benefit the sponsor, either directly or indirectly'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when analyzing state or military communications: check for targeted appeals intended to benefit the sponsor and consider doctrine-driven communication strategies like psychological operations.
